title: From the Editor — The Useful Lie
settingText: Bellweather in light rain: weathered family houses, wet dust, covered porch tables, dim warm windows, mourning cloth and ordinary domestic objects. No funeral body, no identity reveal, no identifiable cast close-ups.
summary: Art-directed opening editorial splash for Sunforge Outlaw Issue 5. Entice the reader, establish the live pressure and world feeling, and preserve the story page-one reveal.

panelPlan.text: SINGLE FULL-PAGE ART-DIRECTED SPLASH. Use one cinematic illustration rather than sequential panels. Reserve a large, deliberately quiet field for the supplied editorial body copy. The illustration supports the text without depicting the next issue's reveal literally.

LETTERING LAYOUT. Treat the supplied CAPTION lines as designed editorial typography, not speech balloons: strong heading, readable body copy, generous leading and margins, and a prominent final hook line. Do not invent any additional text, logos, signage, credits or slogans.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: FROM THE EDITOR

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: They found the people behind the trick.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: That should have made everything simpler.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: Raina James had a theory. Samuel Hayes helped test it. Real names, real grievances, carefully placed expectations. Put Brandon in front of the right wound and see what he knows.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: Some of the road can now be explained.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: Unfortunately, not the beginning.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: And not everything after it.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: There is one more story Samuel set in motion before the truth caught up with him.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: It is waiting at Bellweather.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: So is a family burying one of its own.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: — Jeff Hines

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: Star Splitter Visions

title: One More Setup
summary: At a roadside camp after the relay, Raina admits Samuel set one more identity in motion before the operation was exposed: Nathan Bell at Bellweather.

panelPlan.text: Raina lays Samuel's route notes on a blanket beside the fire. Most entries are crossed through. One remains circled: NATHAN BELL — BELLWEATHER.
Samuel explains he visited Bellweather before the relay confrontation and told one cousin Nathan might return.
Brandon asks whether anyone there is likely to mistake his arrival for good news.
Samuel says Nathan's mother has just died and the wake is underway.

dialogueInline.speaker: Raina
dialogueInline.text: There is one setup still ahead of us.

dialogueInline.speaker: Samuel
dialogueInline.text: Bellweather. Nathan Bell.

dialogueInline.speaker: Brandon
dialogueInline.text: What did you tell them?

dialogueInline.speaker: Samuel
dialogueInline.text: That a man matching Nathan might come home.

dialogueInline.speaker: Brandon
dialogueInline.text: And now his mother is dead.

dialogueInline.speaker: Samuel
dialogueInline.text: The wake started yesterday.

title: Why Go
summary: The obvious choice is to avoid Bellweather. Brandon chooses the opposite because Samuel has already placed his face inside a grieving family's expectations and he does not want the lie growing in his absence.

panelPlan.text: Jessie points out a clean detour on the route map that would take them nowhere near Bellweather.
Eva expects Brandon to take it because he has spent weeks refusing other people's identities.
Brandon folds the Bellweather note and gives it back to Samuel.
He asks the distance rather than the detour.

dialogueInline.speaker: Jessie
dialogueInline.text: We can go around.

dialogueInline.speaker: Brandon
dialogueInline.text: They are already waiting for a man who looks like me.

dialogueInline.speaker: Eva
dialogueInline.text: You want to walk into it on purpose.

dialogueInline.speaker: Brandon
dialogueInline.text: I want them to stop waiting for me on purpose.

dialogueInline.speaker: Samuel
dialogueInline.text: I can go first and undo it.

dialogueInline.speaker: Jessie
dialogueInline.text: You are done going first.

title: Rain on Bellweather
summary: The trio reaches Bellweather in light rain while Raina and Samuel deliberately remain behind on the road, giving Brandon a chance to correct the expectation without the manipulators entering first.

panelPlan.text: Bellweather appears through light rain: close family houses around covered courtyards, long tables and practical workspaces.
Mourning cloth and food trays make the wake visible as ordinary communal labor rather than spectacle.
Raina and Samuel stop the rig at the settlement edge and remain outside the family courtyard by prior agreement.
Brandon, Eva and Jessie walk in through wet dust together.

dialogueInline.speaker: Raina
dialogueInline.text: We'll stay outside unless somebody asks for us.

dialogueInline.speaker: Brandon
dialogueInline.text: That would be a useful change.

dialogueInline.speaker: Samuel
dialogueInline.text: I earned that.

dialogueInline.speaker: Jessie
dialogueInline.text: Then earn the next hour too.

title: Nathan
summary: Mary Bell sees Brandon and reacts with exhausted relief. Owen reacts with suspicion. Brandon gives his real name before either sibling can complete the welcome home.

panelPlan.text: Mary crosses the courtyard carrying a serving bowl, sees Brandon and stops so abruptly another relative nearly walks into her.
Owen rises from a covered table more slowly, studying Brandon rather than embracing the recognition.
Brandon removes his hat out of respect for the wake.
He states his name before Mary can reach him.

dialogueInline.speaker: Mary Bell
dialogueInline.text: Nathan?

dialogueInline.speaker: Brandon
dialogueInline.text: I'm Brandon Mack. I'm sorry someone told you otherwise.

dialogueInline.speaker: Owen Bell
dialogueInline.text: He said you'd deny it.

dialogueInline.speaker: Mary Bell
dialogueInline.text: You look exactly like him.

dialogueInline.speaker: Brandon
dialogueInline.text: I'm sorry for that too.

title: The Empty Place
summary: The Bell family has left Nathan's customary place open at the wake because Samuel's prediction made his return feel plausible again. Brandon's arrival turns an old absence into a fresh family conflict.

panelPlan.text: At the long covered table, one seat near the end has clearly been kept open while every other place is in use.
Mary explains Nathan left years ago after a fight with Owen and never returned.
Owen says their mother kept expecting Nathan until she died.
Brandon refuses the empty chair and takes an ordinary place at the side of the table.

dialogueInline.speaker: Mary Bell
dialogueInline.text: She kept that place for him every year.

dialogueInline.speaker: Owen Bell
dialogueInline.text: Then the preacher came and told us Nathan was finally on the road.

dialogueInline.speaker: Brandon
dialogueInline.text: He should not have done that.

dialogueInline.speaker: Mary Bell
dialogueInline.text: You came anyway.

dialogueInline.speaker: Brandon
dialogueInline.text: Because he did it.

title: What Nathan Heard
summary: The siblings reveal why Nathan's return matters beyond grief. Their mother made an unwritten promise about two houses, and both sides claim Nathan was the only other person present.

panelPlan.text: The conversation shifts when a tenant family crosses the courtyard carrying covered dishes. Owen watches them go.
Mary explains their mother promised that family permanent use of two houses on Bell land.
Owen says no written record exists and the houses are needed by younger Bell relatives.
Both remember Nathan being present during the original conversation, but disagree on what he heard.

dialogueInline.speaker: Mary Bell
dialogueInline.text: Mom promised those two houses would stay with the Calder family.

dialogueInline.speaker: Owen Bell
dialogueInline.text: Mary remembers a promise. I remember a conversation about helping them through winter.

dialogueInline.speaker: Eva
dialogueInline.text: Nathan was there?

dialogueInline.speaker: Mary Bell
dialogueInline.text: He was standing beside her.

dialogueInline.speaker: Owen Bell
dialogueInline.text: Which is why we needed him to come home and say what she actually said.

title: Two Houses
summary: The housing dispute is not a cartoon conflict: Bellweather has real crowding, the Calder family has lived in the houses for years, and honoring or rejecting the promise will affect living people immediately.

panelPlan.text: Mary walks the trio past the two modest houses. Children move between them and a shared work yard; the Calder family is clearly embedded in Bellweather life.
Owen points out two Bell households sharing cramped rooms nearby after marriages and births.
Jessie recognizes that both sides are arguing from actual need, not greed versus virtue.
Brandon asks why the family waited for Nathan instead of deciding after their mother died.

dialogueInline.speaker: Owen Bell
dialogueInline.text: Nobody is throwing them into the road. We need the houses too.

dialogueInline.speaker: Mary Bell
dialogueInline.text: They built half the roofs in this courtyard.

dialogueInline.speaker: Jessie
dialogueInline.text: Both things can be true.

dialogueInline.speaker: Brandon
dialogueInline.text: Then why does one absent man get to settle it?

dialogueInline.speaker: Mary Bell
dialogueInline.text: Because he heard her promise.

title: Owen's Version
summary: Owen privately explains that Nathan had a habit of siding with their mother after arguments, which makes him doubt that Nathan would have been a neutral witness even if he returned.

panelPlan.text: Owen finds Brandon repairing a loose porch rail because standing idle at the wake makes Brandon uncomfortable.
He admits he does not actually trust Nathan's judgment; he trusts the idea that Nathan heard the exact words.
Owen says Mary has turned their mother's kindness into a permanent legal promise after the death.
Eva listens from the steps, realizing the missing brother has become a tool for both siblings.

dialogueInline.speaker: Owen Bell
dialogueInline.text: Nathan would probably take Mary's side. He usually did when Mom was involved.

dialogueInline.speaker: Brandon
dialogueInline.text: Then why are you waiting for him?

dialogueInline.speaker: Owen Bell
dialogueInline.text: Because he was there. I want the words, not his opinion.

dialogueInline.speaker: Eva
dialogueInline.text: Unless the words still need somebody to interpret them.

dialogueInline.speaker: Owen Bell
dialogueInline.text: That is exactly what I am tired of doing.

title: Mary's Version
summary: Mary admits that Nathan's testimony matters to her partly because she wants one final decision that sounds like their mother rather than a negotiation after her death.

panelPlan.text: Mary and Jessie stack dishes under the awning while rain strengthens briefly.
Mary says her mother spent years making sure nobody in Bellweather was left without shelter.
Brandon joins with another tray and asks whether Mary knows what her mother wanted or needs Nathan to make Owen accept it.
Mary admits the distinction is uncomfortable.

dialogueInline.speaker: Mary Bell
dialogueInline.text: I know what she meant.

dialogueInline.speaker: Brandon
dialogueInline.text: Do you need Nathan because you doubt it, or because Owen does?

dialogueInline.speaker: Mary Bell
dialogueInline.text: I need one thing not to become an argument the moment she's gone.

dialogueInline.speaker: Jessie
dialogueInline.text: That may not be something Nathan could give you.

title: The Witness They Want
summary: The family formally asks Brandon to stand in Nathan's place long enough to say what their mother promised. Brandon refuses to manufacture testimony, even though one sentence could temporarily settle the dispute.

panelPlan.text: At the wake table, Owen places a small family token near Brandon and asks him to repeat what Nathan supposedly heard.
Mary does not stop Owen because she wants the same answer for different reasons.
Brandon leaves the token untouched.
The Calder family remains within earshot, making the cost of any invented answer immediate.

dialogueInline.speaker: Owen Bell
dialogueInline.text: Tell us what Mom said about the houses.

dialogueInline.speaker: Brandon
dialogueInline.text: I didn't hear her.

dialogueInline.speaker: Mary Bell
dialogueInline.text: If you would only say she promised—

dialogueInline.speaker: Brandon
dialogueInline.text: Then you would have a witness you know is false.

dialogueInline.speaker: Owen Bell
dialogueInline.text: You expect us to believe you forgot your own mother?

dialogueInline.speaker: Brandon
dialogueInline.text: I expect you to believe I'm not your brother.

title: A Useful Lie
summary: Away from the family, Eva argues that Brandon could lie once for a humane result. Her case is not foolish: the lie might genuinely prevent an ugly dispute.

panelPlan.text: Behind the Bell house near water jars, Eva catches Brandon and Jessie out of earshot of the wake.
She argues that nobody is asking Brandon to steal money or hurt anyone; they want confirmation of a promise that Mary plausibly remembers.
Brandon listens rather than dismissing her.
Eva makes the strongest version of her case: if the lie protects a vulnerable family and ends grief-driven fighting, why privilege factual purity over the result.

dialogueInline.speaker: Eva
dialogueInline.text: You could help them with one sentence.

dialogueInline.speaker: Brandon
dialogueInline.text: By lying.

dialogueInline.speaker: Eva
dialogueInline.text: Once. For people who already believe the promise was real.

dialogueInline.speaker: Eva
dialogueInline.text: If the lie keeps a family in their home, what exactly gets worse?

title: The Second Lie
summary: Brandon and Jessie show Eva why a useful impersonation does not end at the desired sentence. The family would immediately ask what else Nathan remembers, wants and owes.

panelPlan.text: Brandon asks Eva what he should say when Owen asks about Nathan's fight with him, their mother's last year, or where Nathan has been.
Eva proposes refusing those questions. Jessie points out that refusal itself becomes part of the false performance.
The three can hear the wake continuing through the wall, keeping the debate tied to people rather than abstraction.
Eva sees that the lie would create obligations beyond the houses.

dialogueInline.speaker: Brandon
dialogueInline.text: What happens when Owen asks why his brother stayed away?

dialogueInline.speaker: Eva
dialogueInline.text: You say you don't remember.

dialogueInline.speaker: Jessie
dialogueInline.text: Then you need a second lie to protect the first one.

dialogueInline.speaker: Brandon
dialogueInline.text: And a third when Mary asks whether I came back to stay.

dialogueInline.speaker: Eva
dialogueInline.text: I was trying to solve the houses.

dialogueInline.speaker: Jessie
dialogueInline.text: The family does not stop existing after the houses are settled.

title: After We Leave
summary: Jessie identifies the flaw in Eva's urgency: she wants the conflict resolved before the travelers depart, which is not the same as making the community's next day more durable.

panelPlan.text: Eva argues that leaving the dispute open also has consequences.
Jessie agrees, but says a neat ending for travelers can become a mess for residents after the rig is gone.
Brandon says the lie is especially dangerous because it would probably work.
Eva absorbs the point without instantly agreeing with every implication.

dialogueInline.speaker: Eva
dialogueInline.text: Doing nothing has consequences too.

dialogueInline.speaker: Jessie
dialogueInline.text: Of course it does.

dialogueInline.speaker: Jessie
dialogueInline.text: But you want the argument finished before we leave. That is not the same thing as helping them live with the answer.

dialogueInline.speaker: Brandon
dialogueInline.text: The lie is dangerous because they would believe it.

dialogueInline.speaker: Eva
dialogueInline.text: I still don't like leaving them with the fight.

title: The Wake Keeps Going
summary: The wake continues despite the unresolved dispute. Ordinary mourning gives the siblings moments where they are brother and sister rather than opposing claims, opening space for a solution not centered on Nathan.

panelPlan.text: Family members tell stories about the dead mother over supper. Mary and Owen laugh at the same embarrassing memory despite themselves.
Brandon helps serve food and is treated increasingly as a guest rather than Nathan by people who heard his correction.
Eva notices the Calder family contributing stories about the dead woman too, confirming they belong to the community's memory.
Owen quietly brings one of the Calder children a dry blanket when rain blows under the awning.

dialogueInline.speaker: Relative
dialogueInline.text: She once locked Owen out because he called her soup thin.

dialogueInline.speaker: Owen Bell
dialogueInline.text: It was thin.

dialogueInline.speaker: Mary Bell
dialogueInline.text: You slept in the tool shed for defending that opinion.

dialogueInline.speaker: Brandon
dialogueInline.text: I am learning a great deal about this family without becoming part of it.

title: Samuel Comes In
summary: Mary learns Samuel is waiting outside Bellweather and demands that he come explain why he prepared the family for Nathan's return.

panelPlan.text: Mary overhears Eva mention Samuel and realizes the preacher is nearby.
She sends a younger relative to fetch him rather than allowing the travelers to manage the confrontation for her.
Samuel enters the covered courtyard with Raina behind him and recognizes Mary immediately.
Mary sets down the dish in her hands before speaking, controlling her anger enough not to turn the wake into spectacle.

dialogueInline.speaker: Mary Bell
dialogueInline.text: You told us my brother was coming home.

dialogueInline.speaker: Samuel
dialogueInline.text: I did.

dialogueInline.speaker: Mary Bell
dialogueInline.text: You described this man.

dialogueInline.speaker: Samuel
dialogueInline.text: I did that too.

dialogueInline.speaker: Mary Bell
dialogueInline.text: Then you can explain why you thought my grief was a useful place to put him.

dialogueInline.speaker: Samuel
dialogueInline.text: I can explain it. I cannot make it decent.

title: The Blue Room
summary: Mary repeats the private phrase she remembers Samuel using: 'the blue room stays open.' Samuel insists he never heard or said it, creating the first post-reveal detail that falls outside his admitted manipulation.

panelPlan.text: Mary tells Samuel there is one part of his visit she has replayed since the relay story broke.
She quotes the phrase 'the blue room stays open,' explaining it was a family phrase connected to the disputed houses.
Samuel's face loses its practiced social ease. He asks her to repeat when he supposedly said it.
Raina opens Samuel's old route notebook before anyone asks her to.

dialogueInline.speaker: Mary Bell
dialogueInline.text: You looked at me and said, 'the blue room stays open.'

dialogueInline.speaker: Samuel
dialogueInline.text: I never said that.

dialogueInline.speaker: Mary Bell
dialogueInline.text: I remember where you were standing.

dialogueInline.speaker: Samuel
dialogueInline.text: I believe you remember hearing it. I did not know that phrase.

dialogueInline.speaker: Raina
dialogueInline.text: Let me see the page from that visit.

title: The Missing Detail
summary: Samuel's contemporaneous notes contain the Bell family, Nathan and the housing dispute but not the blue-room phrase. Raina treats the absence as a problem to investigate rather than immediate proof of the uncanny.

panelPlan.text: Raina reads Samuel's dated Bellweather notes line by line at the table.
The notes contain Nathan's description, Mary's concern, Owen's skepticism and the fact that houses are disputed, but no private phrase.
Samuel explains he intentionally wrote down unusual phrases when he heard them because such details were useful to the tests.
Raina asks who else could have spoken to Mary before or after Samuel's visit.

dialogueInline.speaker: Raina
dialogueInline.text: You wrote down the houses. You wrote down Nathan's scar. You did not write down a blue room.

dialogueInline.speaker: Samuel
dialogueInline.text: If I had heard that phrase, I would have kept it.

dialogueInline.speaker: Eva
dialogueInline.text: Because it would have made the setup stronger.

dialogueInline.speaker: Samuel
dialogueInline.text: Exactly.

dialogueInline.speaker: Jessie
dialogueInline.text: Then start with ordinary explanations before we invent another one.

title: Start With Family
summary: The group tests the simplest explanations for the blue-room phrase: family repetition, faulty memory and information reaching Mary after Samuel left.

panelPlan.text: Raina asks Mary who knew she was waiting for Nathan after Samuel's visit. The answer is family and the Calders.
Owen says the phrase 'blue room' was their mother's shorthand for keeping one of the houses available to the Calders, but he never discussed it with Samuel.
Several relatives remember the phrase existing; none remembers telling the preacher.
The inquiry remains messy enough that ordinary leakage cannot be ruled out.

dialogueInline.speaker: Raina
dialogueInline.text: Who knew the phrase?

dialogueInline.speaker: Owen Bell
dialogueInline.text: Family. The Calders. Anybody around when Mom used it.

dialogueInline.speaker: Mary Bell
dialogueInline.text: Nobody knew Samuel and I had discussed Nathan until after he left.

dialogueInline.speaker: Jessie
dialogueInline.text: That still leaves a lot of people who could have repeated the words.

dialogueInline.speaker: Eva
dialogueInline.text: But not why Mary remembers them coming from Samuel.

title: A Living Witness
summary: An elderly aunt remembers enough of the original housing conversation to shift the Bell dispute away from Nathan. She did not hear every word, but she heard the dead mother say the Calders should not be moved while she lived and that the family should keep the blue room open afterward.

panelPlan.text: During the blue-room inquiry, an elderly Bell aunt interrupts because the phrase has reminded her of the original conversation.
She says she was in the adjoining room and heard parts of the promise, though not the full terms Mary claims.
Owen questions her memory without accusing her of lying. Mary accepts that the recollection is incomplete.
Brandon remains silent because the family finally has evidence that belongs to its own history.

dialogueInline.speaker: Aunt
dialogueInline.text: I heard your mother say the Calders would not be moved while she was alive.

dialogueInline.speaker: Owen Bell
dialogueInline.text: That still isn't permanent.

dialogueInline.speaker: Aunt
dialogueInline.text: I also heard her tell Nathan to keep the blue room open after she was gone.

dialogueInline.speaker: Mary Bell
dialogueInline.text: Why didn't you say this before?

dialogueInline.speaker: Aunt
dialogueInline.text: Nobody asked me. Everybody was waiting for Nathan.

title: Their Decision
summary: Mary and Owen use the partial witness and their own values to make a living decision: the Calders keep the houses, while Bellweather begins planning new space for the crowded Bell households.

panelPlan.text: The siblings speak with the Calder family directly instead of discussing them at another table.
Owen admits the evidence does not prove every detail Mary remembers, but it proves enough that eviction would violate what their mother was trying to protect.
Mary agrees the family must solve its crowding rather than make the Calders absorb it.
Brandon carries chairs back under the awning while the decision happens without him.

dialogueInline.speaker: Owen Bell
dialogueInline.text: I still don't know that Mom meant forever.

dialogueInline.speaker: Mary Bell
dialogueInline.text: Neither do I anymore.

dialogueInline.speaker: Owen Bell
dialogueInline.text: I know she meant you were not supposed to lose your home because she died.

dialogueInline.speaker: Calder
dialogueInline.text: That is enough for tonight.

dialogueInline.speaker: Jessie
dialogueInline.text: Tomorrow can have its own argument.

title: Why the Lie Was Worse
summary: After the wake, Eva revisits her useful-lie argument. Brandon explains that the false testimony would have been worse precisely because it might have ended the discussion before the family found its own evidence and chose its own compromise.

panelPlan.text: Outside after the rain, Eva sits on the rig step while Brandon washes a borrowed plate.
She admits his refusal forced the family to keep looking, which is not the outcome she expected.
Brandon says he could have stopped the argument but could not make the invented answer true.
Jessie listens while securing gear, allowing the conversation to belong primarily to Brandon and Eva.

dialogueInline.speaker: Eva
dialogueInline.text: Your lie would have worked faster.

dialogueInline.speaker: Brandon
dialogueInline.text: That was the problem.

dialogueInline.speaker: Eva
dialogueInline.text: You could have stopped the fighting.

dialogueInline.speaker: Brandon
dialogueInline.text: I could have stopped the argument. I couldn't make tomorrow depend on something true.

dialogueInline.speaker: Eva
dialogueInline.text: You worry a lot about what happens after we leave.

dialogueInline.speaker: Brandon
dialogueInline.text: Somebody should. We keep leaving.

title: The Detail That Stayed
summary: The trio leaves while Raina and Samuel remain to trace the unexplained blue-room memory. The human setup is proven, but one small detail has escaped the mechanism that was supposed to explain it.

panelPlan.text: Raina and Samuel sit with Mary under the awning, building a list of everyone who might have carried the phrase to her.
Samuel is no longer treating the family as a test; he is answering Mary's questions about exactly what he did and did not say.
Eva looks back from the rig but does not return to investigate immediately.
Brandon and Jessie face forward as Bellweather recedes in clear post-rain light.

dialogueInline.speaker: Eva
dialogueInline.text: Do you think Samuel said it and forgot?

dialogueInline.speaker: Jessie
dialogueInline.text: Possible.

dialogueInline.speaker: Eva
dialogueInline.text: Do you think Mary attached it to the wrong memory?

dialogueInline.speaker: Jessie
dialogueInline.text: Also possible.

dialogueInline.speaker: Brandon
dialogueInline.text: Then leave both possibilities alive until you know more.

dialogueInline.speaker: Eva
dialogueInline.text: I am getting better at that.

title: Next: BRANNOCK STAYED
settingText: A long road curling back toward the Last Drop. In the far distance, the exterior wall with its crude human mural catches the last light. The returning travelers remain tiny and unidentifiable.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: Samuel planted the story.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: Then Bellweather gave it a detail he never knew.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: That leaves one clean place to test the theory:

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: the first mistake.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: No preacher.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: No Raina.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: No setup.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: The Last Drop.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: Brandon left.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: Brannock stayed.

dialogueInline.speaker: CAPTION
dialogueInline.text: NEXT: BRANNOCK STAYED
